Conduct the continuous wavelet transform on a time series/signal

Source: R/analyse_wavelet.R, R/zzz_aliases_american.R
analyse_wavelet.Rd

Compute the continuous wavelet transform (CWT) using a Morlet wavelet

Usage

analyse_wavelet(
  data = NULL,
  dj = 1/100,
  lowerPeriod = 2,
  upperPeriod = 1024,
  verbose = FALSE,
  omega_nr = 8,
  wavelet = "morlet",
  wavelet_order = NULL,
  pval = FALSE,
  n_simulations = 10,
  run_multicore = FALSE,
  n_cores = NULL
)

analyze_wavelet(
  data = NULL,
  dj = 1/100,
  lowerPeriod = 2,
  upperPeriod = 1024,
  verbose = FALSE,
  omega_nr = 8,
  wavelet = "morlet",
  wavelet_order = NULL,
  pval = FALSE,
  n_simulations = 10,
  run_multicore = FALSE,
  n_cores = NULL
)

Arguments

data

Input record: a matrix or data frame with depth/time in column 1 and the proxy value in column 2. Rows with NA are removed, the rows are sorted by depth/time and the record is linearly interpolated to an even spacing equal to the median sampling interval. Required (Default=NULL gives an error).

dj

Spacing between successive scales in octaves (numeric, > 0). The periods analysed increase by powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, ...), and dj sets how many steps are made per doubling of the period: dj=1/x gives x periods per octave. Smaller values give a finer period axis but increase the computation time. Default=1/100.

lowerPeriod

Shortest period to analyse, in the same unit as the depth/time column of data (numeric, > 0; at least twice the sampling interval). Together with upperPeriod it sets the range of cycles analysed; because the period axis is log2-scaled, a power of 2 gives the neatest plots. Default=2.

upperPeriod

Longest period to analyse, in the same unit as the depth/time column of data (numeric, > lowerPeriod; normally not more than the length of the record); a power of 2 gives the neatest plots. Default=1024.

verbose

Print the sampling interval to which the record was interpolated and, when pval=TRUE, show a progress bar of the simulations (logical, TRUE or FALSE). Default=FALSE.

omega_nr

Number of cycles of the Morlet wavelet, i.e. its central angular frequency omega_0 (numeric, > 0, typically 5 to 15). A larger value gives a longer wavelet with more oscillations: a better period resolution and a worse depth/time resolution. Also used as the default parameter of "morlet0" and to match the bandwidth of some other wavelets. Default=8.

wavelet

Mother wavelet (character string or function), given as a name (PyWavelets style names with the order appended, such as "db4", "sym8", "cgau3", "gaus2" or "cmor1.5-1", also work) or as a function psi_hat(omega) that returns the Fourier transform of a user defined mother wavelet. Analytic (complex) wavelets, which give phase and amplitude and can be synchrosqueezed: "morlet" (default; aliases "gabor", "amor"), "morlet0" (exactly zero mean Morlet, admissible for a small omega_nr; alias "morlex"), "paul" (alias "cauchy"), "morse" (generalised Morse wavelet of Olhede and Walden, 2002; aliases "gmw", "airy"), "bump", "cmor" (complex Morlet with bandwidth and centre frequency as in Matlab/PyWavelets), "cgau" (analytic Gaussian derivative; "cmhat" is the complex Mexican hat), "shannon" (complex Shannon, box spectrum), "fbsp" (frequency B-spline), "meyer", "loggabor" (alias "lognormal"), "gammatone" (asymmetric in time: sharp onset, slow decay) and "hann" (raised cosine band). Real wavelets, which give a real transform (no phase or envelope): "dog" (derivative of Gaussian; "mexh", "ricker", "marr" and "sombrero" are the Mexican hat, order 2), "morl" (real Morlet), "hhat" (Hermitian hat), "poisson", and the orthogonal wavelets "haar", "db" (Daubechies), "sym" (Symlets) and "battle" (Battle-Lemarie spline wavelets), which are computed in the frequency domain from their filters. The period axis of the orthogonal wavelets is approximate because their spectra are broad and not symmetric. A narrow wavelet (Paul, low-order DOG, Shannon, Haar) resolves position well, a wide one (Morse with a large beta, Morlet with a high omega_nr, bump) resolves period well. Default="morlet".

wavelet_order

Parameter(s) of the wavelet (numeric scalar or vector; NULL uses the defaults listed here): paul: order m (default 4); dog: derivative m (default 2); morse: c(gamma, beta) or beta alone with gamma = 3 (default c(3, 20)); bump: c(mu, sigma) (default c(5, 0.6)); cmor: c(bandwidth, centre frequency) (default c(1.5, 1)); cgau: derivative m (default 4); shannon: c(bandwidth, centre frequency) (default c(2, 1.5)); fbsp: c(m, bandwidth, centre frequency) (default c(2, 2, 1.5)); loggabor: c(centre angular frequency, log-width) (default c(6, 0.25)); meyer and hhat have no parameter; morlet0: omega_0 (default omega_nr); morl: omega_0 (default 5); poisson: order n (default 2); gammatone: c(n, centre angular frequency, bandwidth) (default c(4, 6, 1.5)); hann: c(centre angular frequency, half width) (default c(6, 3)); db: number of vanishing moments 1 to 20 (default 4, "haar" = "db1"); sym: 2 to 20 (default 8); battle: spline order 1, 3, 5 or 7 (default 3). For the Morlet wavelet use omega_nr. The period axis is always the Fourier period, i.e. the period of the sinusoid at which the wavelet has its maximum response, so the results of different wavelets are comparable. Default=NULL.

pval

Calculate p-values of the wavelet power by Monte Carlo simulation (logical, TRUE or FALSE). Default=FALSE. Each simulation analyses a surrogate record made of the average of a shuffled copy of the data (white noise) and an AR(1) red-noise series with the mean and standard deviation of the data and a lag-1 autocorrelation drawn around the value estimated in a moving window of half the record length. The shuffled part keeps high-amplitude short-period cycles from becoming significant; the red-noise part gives a spectrum similar to that of the data without being biased by possible astronomical peaks in it. The p-value is the fraction of simulations whose power is at least the observed power (returned as Power.pval and Power.avg.pval).

n_simulations

Number of Monte Carlo simulations used for the p-values (integer, > 0); only used when pval=TRUE. More simulations give more precise p-values but take longer. Default=10.

run_multicore

Run the Monte Carlo simulations in parallel on several cores (logical, TRUE or FALSE); only used when pval=TRUE. Default=FALSE.

n_cores

Number of cores used when run_multicore=TRUE (integer, > 0); NULL picks an automatic, safe number: physical cores minus one, at most 4, and limited by the free memory. Set options(waverider.n_cores = ...) to change that default. A value > 1 also switches on parallel computing. Results do not depend on the number of cores. Default=NULL.

Value

The output is a list (wavelet object) which contain 20 objects which are the result of the continuous wavelet transform (CWT). Object 1: Wave - Wave values of the wavelet Object 2: Phase - Phase of the wavelet Object 3: Ampl - Amplitude values of the wavelet Object 4: Power - Power values of the wavelet Object 5: dt - Step size Object 6: dj - Scale size Object 7: Power.avg - Average power values Object 8: Period - Period values Object 9: Scale - Scale value Object 10: coi.1 - Cone of influence values 1 Object 11: coi.2 - Cone of influence values 2 Object 12: nc - Number of columns Object 13: nr - Number of rows Object 14: axis.1 - axis values 1 Object 15: axis.2 - axis values 2 Object 16: omega_nr - Number of cycles in the wavelet Object 17: x - x values of the data set Object 18: y - y values of the data set Object 19: average p value of the spectral power Object 20: p value of spectral power

References

Angi Roesch and Harald Schmidbauer (2018). WaveletComp: Computational Wavelet Analysis. R package version 1.1. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=WaveletComp

Gouhier TC, Grinsted A, Simko V (2021). R package biwavelet: Conduct Univariate and Bivariate Wavelet Analyses. (Version 0.20.21), https://github.com/tgouhier/biwavelet

Torrence, C., and G. P. Compo. 1998. A Practical Guide to Wavelet Analysis. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 79:61-78. https://paos.colorado.edu/research/wavelets/bams_79_01_0061.pdf

Morlet, Jean, Georges Arens, Eliane Fourgeau, and Dominique Glard. "Wave propagation and sampling theory—Part I: Complex signal and scattering in multilayered media. " Geophysics 47, no. 2 (1982): 203-221.

J. Morlet, G. Arens, E. Fourgeau, D. Giard; Wave propagation and sampling theory; Part II, Sampling theory and complex waves. Geophysics 1982 47 (2): 222–236.

Author

Code based on on the "WaveletComp" function of the 'WaveletComp' R package and "wt" function of the 'biwavelet' R package which are based on the wavelet MATLAB code written by Christopher Torrence and Gibert P. Compo.

Examples

# \donttest{
#Example 1. Using the Total Solar Irradiance data set of Steinhilver et al., (2012)
TSI_wt <-
 analyse_wavelet(
   data = TSI,
   dj = 1/200,
   lowerPeriod = 16,
   upperPeriod = 8192,
   verbose = FALSE,
   omega_nr = 6,
   pval=FALSE,
   n_simulations=10,
   run_multicore = FALSE
 )


#Example 2. Using the magnetic susceptibility data set of Pas et al., (2018)
mag_wt <-
analyse_wavelet(
data = mag,
dj = 1/100,
lowerPeriod = 0.1,
upperPeriod = 254,
verbose = FALSE,
omega_nr = 10,
pval=FALSE,
n_simulations=10,
run_multicore = FALSE
)

#Example 3. Using the greyscale data set of Zeeden et al., (2013)
grey_wt <-
 analyse_wavelet(
   data = grey,
   dj = 1/200,
   lowerPeriod = 0.02,
   upperPeriod = 256,
   verbose = FALSE,
   omega_nr = 8,
   pval=FALSE,
   n_simulations=10,
   run_multicore = FALSE
 )

# }
